utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon once again, everybody. Mr. Registrar, may you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Appearances for today? For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Matthias Neuner, Laurie Sartorio, assisted today by our intern Shona McJannett and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Witness, may I just warn you, you may be aware of it but it's the duty of the Trial Chamber to warn you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much. I beg your pardon. Madam Vidovic, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record, I would like to say that the Defence counsel is present, Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson with their associates, Lejla Gluhic, Asja Zujo and our intern Chloe McRae.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic, and I'm awfully sorry for that slight omission. Yesterday, Judge Lattanzi had just finished asking her questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you testified during cross-examination that the Mujahedin distributed food to the local Muslim population. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did they distribute food to the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because in that particular area there were no Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So -- okay. Are you aware of them having distributed food to any Croats where there were Croats?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That information was not available to me, and I myself never went to such areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also testified that you were 100 per cent certain that no Arab was a member of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that there were none in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you said your brigade, what were you actually referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 306th, the brigade that I belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were members of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you also talked about lack of support from the judiciary, in terms of prosecuting crimes. For me, who doesn't understand the system, I would like to understand. If somebody commits a crime out there, at what stage does the judiciary intervene? I guess the gravimen of my question is does the judiciary go and arrest, or is the person arrested by the police and brought to the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the courts did not issue any orders, unless it was known for sure that a military person was involved. In that case we would bring that person in and the Court would take over from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the people that we are talking about were military people, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The people who you are testifying about as having committed crimes were people who committed crimes as members of the military?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not registered as military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In my view, they were paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you say the courts did not issue orders, any orders, what orders were these that were supposed to be issued?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders for arrest, or arrest warrants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But my question is, then, had these arrest warrants been sought from the Court?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were valid arguments, if there was information sent to the Court, the Court would have issued an arrest warrant. However, while I was there, we did not have such situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But understand my question. My question is not if. I want to know whether, in fact, such warrants were sought from the Court.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never approached the Court. The only time we would address the Court for anything was when we filed a criminal report, and only if we had done that, the Court would follow up and would come back to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is: Did you file those criminal reports with the Court?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, yes. But those criminal reports were filed for the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "later on," what do you mean? Because I'm asking you at the time when you say the courts were inefficient and not giving you any support, I want to know that did you file these reports with the judiciary and the judiciary just didn't do anything about them or what happened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the event in Bikosi maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, that included, yes. That included all crimes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to Bikosi, we did not file any reports because we did not have any information. So the reports were not filed. The only reports that I'm aware of were reports filed against our people who failed to respond to the call-up or committed thefts or even murders at some instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's deal with them one by one. Now, with respect to the Bikosi incident, you can therefore not say that you didn't get any support from the judiciary because you did not file any reports with the judiciary; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With respect to the local Bosnian military who were not answering call-ups, did you file any reports with the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was the response of the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some positive developments, there were some negative developments. It happened sometimes that the criminal report was turned down because there were no valid foundations for such criminal reports, and the courts simply did not prosecute those people or found them innocent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if there were no valid foundations for the reports, can it be said that the judiciary was not lending support, or did the people who filed reports not do their job properly to satisfy the Court that there was a need to take steps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question. I believe that the problem was a lack of professionalism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On whose part?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the part of the service that was in charge of filing those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, the blame cannot be put on the Court, sir; am I right? You should be able to answer that question because it's a logical question based on what you're telling us. Blame cannot be put on the courts.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have just told us there was lack of professionalism on the part of the people who filed the reports. What was the lack of professionalism, the lack of professionalism was that they filed reports which did not have a valid foundation for a warrant of arrest to be issued. Who is to blame, sir? Is it the Court or is it the person who files an unfounded report?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I leave it at that. I guess it's more of a rhetorical question anyway. Now, you also testified that there were groups of Arabs who had not joined the Mujahedin. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did those groups that had not joined Mujahedin fight alongside with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you aware of any Mujahedins fighting alongside the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the area where we were deployed, there were none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Talking about the civilians who were in camps, in the camp in Mehurici and other places, you said that they were the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior and not of the army. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the status of these people? Why were they kept in these camps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a camp. We called it an acceptance or reception centre where people were accommodated in order to be protected, so they were there for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whose responsibility is to see to the safety of people who have surrendered in times of war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior was responsible; although, we also helped out with a few people that were provided for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But my question is, if you do know the answer to it, more of a legal question, not actually what took place on the ground. Where people in time of war surrender to the army, your army, whose responsibility is it in law to look after those people?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were these civilians who were in this [Microphone not activated] Were these civilians who were in the reception centre free to leave the centre any time they wished to? Could they just walk out if they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could leave but they didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also testified, sir, yesterday that you told your superiors about the problems from the Mujahedin. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you referring to? Can you please jog my memory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I know now the transcript will have changed. It was page 105 of yesterday's transcript at lines 5 and 6. I don't know whether we are able to determine what page it would be today. But you testified at that point in time that you made reports, you told your superiors, about the problems that you were receiving from Mujahedin, and I just want to ask you a few questions about that statement. Do you remember saying so?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. If you do there is no need to look for it on the transcript. Now, did you receive any reaction from your superiors to the reports that you gave them about these problems?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you, sir. Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench, Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just following up on what Your Honour has just asked, whether any response from superiors with regard to the problems with the Mujahedin were coming, could I have, please, Exhibit PT 1500 being shown to the witness? Further re-examination by Mr. Neuner:

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The first page, please. This is a document from the 26th of August 1993 or it was sent on the 26th of August 1993. Is there also an English translation available? There is no English translation available? Well, I have one but it is marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe, Witness, you can read out the relevant line. First of all your name, it just disappears, if you could scroll down a little bit, type signed is your name Osman Fusko, do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Asim Delalic signed instead of me because at the at the end of the day he was the person who was authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having looked at the document today, do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly, but I could not quote the contents off my head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it assist you if I just tried to summarise? It relates to arson, alleged arson, and it says in the document, "The perpetrators of this act are Mujahedin." Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to explore is one line, which is about the fourth line from the bottom. "We have repeatedly reported this." Do you find this in the Bosnian language, and if you could please read it, then, out for the benefit of everybody in and around the courtroom. Could you please read this sentence out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For a long time now, members of the Mujahedin are creating a lot of problems."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can interrupt, I'm just referring to the one sentence starting with "we have repeated" -- I'm sorry, I interrupted you. If you could please go on.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to continue where I left it off? "For a long time now, members of the Mujahedin have been creating a lot of problems which we have informed you a lot of times, and we have still not received any instruction as to how to deal with this problem, although, we have requested, I informed you and asked for your assistance with this matter. We sincerely hope that you will take this under advisement because we are really at a loss as to how to deal with this problem, and we expect help from you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is this letter addressed to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you could scroll up in the original document, it is addressed, as far as I could see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you, to whom was the letter addressed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosanska Krajina OG, operative group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was this operative group based in 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the relationship between your unit, the 306th Brigade, and the OG Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're addressing this to the OG Bosanska Krajina. I'm just inquiring why did you send it to the OG Bosanska Krajina? What was the relationship to this unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosanska Krajina OG was our immediate superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having sent this letter and formulating your request to them to receive precise instruction, did you manage to receive instructions?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that any specific instructions ever reached us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to touch briefly on an issue which was addressed yesterday by Judge Harhoff. I wish to -- before I do this, I wish to tender this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are you going to provide a translation of this, an English translation, which is not marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. I was just informed that the translation of this document is on page 2 of this exhibit as it was uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Maybe it is possible to split that up into two pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Then this document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to move on to another area, Judge Harhoff yesterday addressed the issue of a possible cover-up. This is page 101, line 12 of yesterday's transcript. And I wish to explore further who may have been involved in requesting your report from the 19th of October, that this report be produced, and who may have consumed the information you provided in this report. Can, please, Exhibit 140 be shown again? Witness, who are the addressees of your report?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the same, the Bosanska Krajina OG.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says -- what entity within the OG Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the security organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can also point you to number 3 on the lower left-hand corner of the document, it says, "3 Korpus" there. Why is this stated there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All documents were sent in this way, to the OG, and the 3rd Corps because the 3rd Corps was our main command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time, why did you send this document to both entities? Why did you inform both entities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All documents were sent according to the same system, and this was the system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Delalic gave you instructions to write this report, was there anybody else around?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody was around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having received these instructions from Mr. Delalic, what was your impression? Who, in fact, was the spiritual author of these instructions?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delalic. Who else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had drafted your report, had anybody else the chance to see it before it was processed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Probably this happened in the late afternoon, when nobody else was around. There were people in the command but no one apart from the security had the right to see this, and the lads working on sending out the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had signed this report for Mr. Delalic. Did Mr. Delalic at some later point in time inquire whether you had indeed followed all his instructions given?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was available to him at any moment for him to inspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the issue again?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not especially, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn to another point, the presence of the Mujahedin in Bila valley. Judge Lattanzi mentioned yesterday that the presence -- or asked yesterday whether the presence of the Mujahedin in the valley of Bila may have been authorised by some higher authority. And this is on page 106, line 7 to 10. I wish to explore this further. And I want to show you Exhibit the 136. Could this please be shown? You have seen this document yesterday already. It dates from the 13th of May, and it is type-signed by your superior, Asim Delalic, and I'm asking you to look at the seventh line of this document. It's equal in English as well as in B/C/S. The seventh line of the main text says, "On 11th of May 1993, the assistant commander for security affairs and the 306th bbr commander were at a meeting with the Mujahedin where we received information supplied to us by their Emir. Representatives of the Mujahedin have spoken to Mr. Sefer Halilovic personally, and they have another meeting in a few days time regarding the formation of the brigade." My question is: In May 1993, what position did Sefer Halilovic hold?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the commander at that time of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Neuner. Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also have a few questions and I will start from this last document, if it can be kept for a while. Document 136. Further cross-examination by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have seen this document. You saw it yesterday and today. The document states that allegedly the Mujahedin said they had spoken to Sefer Halilovic about establishing the 8th Muslim Brigade. Witness, to the best of your knowledge, did the Muslim -- or, rather, was the 8th Muslim Brigade ever established within the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Have you ever heard of it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now I will go back to document 140.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness look at document 140 again? It is a document we discussed at length yesterday, but I want the witness to see it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, evidently you spoke to Mr. Asim Delalic about drawing up this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'll put open-ended questions to you, no leading questions. Please answer to the best of your ability. Did you ever at any point in that conversation understand Mr. Delalic to be suggesting you conceal anything?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with reference to your testimony about this document, in a response to questions from all the parties, Their Honours, the Prosecution, myself, yesterday and again today, you said you were given instructions as to how to draft this letter. You explained to Their Honours that in the instructions given to you by Mr. Delalic, he said that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not committed a crime. You repeated that more than once yesterday.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His Honour, Judge Moloto, on page 94 of the transcript, lines 13 to 16, said, I quote, "Now you are giving us a new testimony, something you never said before, which is not in this letter." And that was after my question about Mr. Delalic's instructions, when he told you that the army had not committed any crimes. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Witness, I will read to you your response, which you gave to the Prosecutor's question on page 82, line 5. I quote, Prosecutor, "Can you explain how you wrote this document?" And your response, "The document was drawn up in accordance with the request sent to us. I consulted Asim Delalic. I asked him what we should do. He told me to write a report; that is, information saying that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not committed any crimes, and that nothing -- none of those things were done by members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that she does not have the original transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what you answered on page 52 to a question by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is in fact the truth, is it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not commit any crimes?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you explained that this is not in the document, but that that is how you understood inter alia a part of his instructions?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'll ask you something else, Witness. It's correct, is it not, that when you were writing this report, you had before you, the letter from the higher command, the superior command. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether I had it before me or not. Probably there had been requests arriving earlier, and Delalic said we should draw up this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly, Witness. More than once yesterday, in the course of your testimony, you said, "I was responding to a request." So now I want to ask you the following: Was the request about asking whether units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were involved in the crime?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be sure, but I think that's what it was about, yes. I don't have the text or the request in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a lot of time has elapsed, so I can't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you draw up a response to a request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there was a request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'll ask you something that follows from questions put by the Prosecutor and Their Honours. It's correct, is it not, that neither you nor Mr. Delalic had any professional knowledge as to how to conduct an investigation and how to write this kind of document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just Delalic and myself. None of us had that kind of professional knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Further Questions by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Fusko, if I may follow up on some of counsel Vidovic's questions, and I'm sorry to return to this matter, but the reason I'm doing it is that I think that there is something, what should I say, fishy about the ways in which crimes committed in your area of responsibility were reported up through the system of command. In Exhibit 145, which is dated the 26th of February 1993, we had -- that was the document that was shown to you on the screen just a little while ago, it was the document in which you were complaining about arson committed by the Mujahedin and seeking instructions and which I understand you had drafted but Delalic had signed on your behalf. Apparently arson had been committed, you were believing that it was committed by Mujahedin, and you were complaining about it, and you were seeking instructions from the operative group. This was in February. In October that same year, eight months later, we hear of a possible massacre being committed in Bikosi, and the response this time from your side was that no crime was committed, these victims were all combatants and if anything, it was certainly not committed by members of your army. And I find it surprising, based on your testimony yesterday, when I asked you about the massacre in Bikosi, if that had not been the talk of the camp these days when the crime was committed. And I was led to believe that everybody had heard about this, and everybody talked about it. Yet, when we came to October, a couple of months later, the report that was sent from you up to the 3rd Corps was, if I may say it, very, very neutral. The answer that you gave was that no crimes had been committed and nothing wrong had been committed by your army. And I ask you again: Why is there such a difference when, in February, you were seeking instructions of how to handle the crime of arson, presumably committed by Mujahedin, while in October, when there was a possibility at least of a major crime, a massacre of 30 people or more, possibly also committed by the Mujahedin, then this time there was silence from your side? I simply don't understand why these two situations were treated so differently. Can you help us explain what to me appears to be a contradiction? Take your time.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I don't know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sure you have an opinion. You were involved in both reports. Why did you react so differently in February and in October of that same year?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what document is mentioned in February? May I see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, of course, can we have Exhibit 145 brought to the screen? Sorry, I was unable to read the dates on the exhibit, so it appears it was not in February; it was in August. But that just makes my point even more clear because now there is a difference of only two months. So apparently Exhibit 145, your report on the arson, was drafted in August, not in February, and I apologise, I couldn't read, while your report on the Bikosi incident came in October. So only two months later, your way of handling it as the professional policeman seems to me to be so different that I really can't understand what was the reason.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any special explanation to give. I only followed orders. I was just a refer to an officer executing others' orders. I couldn't decide on anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether my learned friends have any additional questions, but I do have a question about the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was going to ask you -- before I ask you, do you, Mr. Neuner? Further re-examination by Mr. Neuner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fusko, in the first -- we have talked about the arson incident. We have talked about the Bikosi incident, which involved the killing. Was there any other killing committed by the Mujahedin in the year of 1993 in the AOR of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was an incident in the village of Miletici, but I know practically nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What little information, if any, do you know about that incident in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that some people were killed, but I don't have any information as to how many or how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Miletici, the village of Miletici has nothing to do with Judge Harhoff's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Well, I respectfully disagree because Judge Harhoff was asking for crimes committed and for the investigation of this witness's military security service into it, and especially for the way how to deal with crimes committing in the AOR of the 306th. In so far I think there is a basis for me to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I'm sorry that the witness has answered before you came up with your objection. Do you have any suggestion what we should do with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only want my objection to be noted on the record, but as the witness has answered, I'm satisfied the witness has said he knows nothing about it, but I beg my learned friends to refrain from similar questions in future and to follow the rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your objection is noted, Madam Vidovic. Thank you very much. Do you have any questions for the witness? Are you done, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He's not done yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, which included inter alia also the incident in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You asked me the same question in the same way as now, and I told you that I heard about it but I wasn't familiar with the details. The whole valley heard that it had happened, but I wasn't there and I can't provide any information about it because I don't have any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you gave your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Vidovic is on her feet. Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I should keep standing because I hardly have time to stand up before the witness begins answering the question. I think the Prosecutor hears my objection, he hears Your Honours upholding it, but then continues putting questions in the same line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, can you restrict yourself to the issues that were before the witness yesterday and that the Judge talked about and not Miletici?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neuner. Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, two brief questions. Further cross-examination by Ms. Vidovic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Exhibit 145 was discussed. That was the last exhibit shown by His Honour Judge Harhoff, dated August 1995. In connection with this document I wish to ask you the following: You said you were just an ordinary referent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not a professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's possible, is it not, that your superior, Mr. Delalic, and the brigade commander superior to him, got some instructions that you know nothing about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Microphone not activated] Witness, thank you so much for coming to testify. On behalf of the Tribunal I give you these thanks. This brings us now to the end of your testimony. You are now excused, and you may stand down. Once again, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Next witness, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise but before this witness comes in, I wish to clarify a certain situation, and hear Your Honour's standpoint. I asked, with respect to the next witness, who will begin his testimony today, in view of the fact that the Prosecutor asked for seven or eight statements to be admitted, which he intends to use in the examination-in-chief, under Rule 92 ter, and I opposed this. After that, I agreed to Your Honour's proposal that the Prosecutor extract the parts he wishes to put to the witness during the examination-in-chief, and that this take six hours. I stated then quite clearly that it would be a problem for me in this short space of time to begin my cross-examination before the recess. In the meantime, I have spoken to my learned friends. It's not clear in the record. We understood this differently. I think I was quite clear when I said that based on such voluminous material, I could not begin my cross-examination if the Prosecutor finishes by Wednesday. The reason for this is that two parts, or rather two groups of documents have been admitted which the Prosecutor wishes to use, most of which are not contained in the statement I received as the basis for the testimony in 2007. I need time not only to read this but to find and deal with and prepare other documents for my cross-examination. This is a very important area. These are very important materials which will help Your Honours understand the case. I received proofing notes yesterday which contain some facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just make your point. You have given us such background. What is your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be very brief, briefly, I wish to begin my cross-examination after the recess. This will give me enough time to prepare for my cross-examination properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was a very long way of coming to that point, Madam Vidovic. You will remember, ma'am, that the Chamber did say to the Prosecution that it allows him -- it allows the Prosecution to do -- to use the full six hours for this witness, which means, in fact, that it is anticipated that the Prosecution is going to be leading this witness until the end of the week, by which time we will go on recess, and you'll have plenty of time to prepare. Okay? Your witness, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be handling this witness. However this witness testified in closed session in another trial, and those protective measures are automatically applicable to this Court, and under the rules, I think it's Rule 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam Sartorio. Did you say in closed session? Not private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: According to the record it says we would go into closed session is the way it was stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, may the Chamber please move into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of July, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
